claims.text: The initial nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt.
The AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution at room temperature.
High-resolution TEM or aberration-corrected STEM can characterize atomic-scale structural rearrangements.
An integrated in situ heating stage enables real-time observation of thermally induced rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
EDS or EELS can track element-specific diffusion and segregation during in situ heating.
Controlled ramped heating can be performed during real-time TEM imaging while ensuring minimal beam-induced artifacts.
Heating induces atomic-scale diffusion and local elemental segregation or ordering in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Increasing temperature gives atoms sufficient energy to overcome kinetic barriers and rearrange.
Temperature-dependent phase-related behavior can occur in high-entropy alloys.
Segregation or phase transformation in AuCoCuNiPt is expected because of the alloy's high configurational entropy.
Observation of thermally induced rearrangements would provide experimental evidence for an entropic stabilization mechanism.
Heating will produce measurable element-specific segregation or minor structural phase transitions relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The observable response may be limited by the temperature range tolerated by the TEM setup and by electron-beam interactions.
Thermal rearrangements may become pronounced only above an unspecified threshold temperature.
The threshold temperatures and magnitudes of atomic rearrangements in these nanoparticles are unknown.
Experimental validation of thermal behavior in noble-metal-based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is lacking.
Room-temperature experiments under identical beam conditions provide a control for separating thermal effects from beam effects.
A lack of statistically significant structural changes or elemental redistribution at elevated temperature would falsify the proposed thermally activated rearrangement hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats segregation or phase transformation as evidence for entropic stabilization, but it does not explain how loss of elemental or structural uniformity demonstrates stabilization rather than destabilization.
The falsification rule treats a null result as decisive, whereas the boundary states that instrumental temperature limits or beam interactions may prevent the relevant response from being observed.
